title: "MCP"

The gateway speaks MCP in both directions: agents can read and drive the plant,
and an automation rule can call a tool somewhere else.

The design rule is that **an agent is a caller like any other**. The tools read
through the same cache the UI reads and write through the same gate the UI
writes through. There is no privileged path, no bypass, and no separate policy.
A write an operator would be refused is refused; a write that succeeds lands in
the same audit table with `mcp:` in front of the actor.

## Serving

### Over HTTP

Enabled by default at `/mcp` on the app's port, protected by a bearer token the
chart generates into the release Secret.

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop get secret <release> \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.mcp-token}' | base64 -d
```

In-cluster, the endpoint is:

```
http://<release>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:8080/mcp
```

The token check sits in front of the handler, so an unauthenticated caller
cannot even enumerate what exists. Leaving `mcp.token` empty makes the chart
generate one, the default deployment is not accidentally the open one. Combine
it with the NetworkPolicy; a token is a second line of defense, not the only one.

The endpoint is never open. Run the binary with no `HOTLOOP_MCP_TOKEN` (a
Quadlet unit, a bare `hotloop`) and it makes a token at its first start and keeps
it in its database, so the same one comes back after a restart, on every replica
and after a restore. `hotloop mcp-token` prints it (the log says it made one, and
never what it is). Set `HOTLOOP_MCP_TOKEN` to choose your own; with
`HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_*` set the endpoint takes a login and keeps no token of its
own. A client that used to connect to a bare binary with nothing now gets a `401`
until it sends `Authorization: Bearer <that token>`.

### With a Vord login or a hub assertion

The static token says which client called; it cannot say which person. With
OIDC set, `/mcp` also takes `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`, and the verified
person's email becomes the audit actor: a write lands as `mcp:pat@example.com`
instead of `mcp:<client name>`. Behavior with it unset is unchanged, and the
static token keeps working beside it (with no static token set, only a verified
JWT gets in).

| Variable | Chart value | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_ISSUER` | `mcp.oidc.issuer` | the Vord realm URL; accepts its access tokens |
| `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_AUDIENCE` | `mcp.oidc.audience` | the `aud` every token must carry; required with either of these |
| `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_HUB_JWKS_URL` | `mcp.oidc.hubJwksUrl` | the identity hub's assertion keys; accepts its assertions |
| `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_REQUIRED_ROLE` | `mcp.oidc.requiredRole` | a realm role the caller must hold |
| `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_WRITE_ROLE` | `mcp.oidc.writeRole` | limits writes per caller, see below |

A Vord access token is checked against the issuer's JWKS (found through its
discovery document, cached ten minutes, refetched on an unknown `kid`): RS256
or ES256 only, `iss` equal to the issuer, `aud` containing the audience, `exp`
and `nbf` with 30 s of skew, and an `email` (or `preferred_username`) claim.
Vord puts only `account` in `aud` by default; give the client scope an
audience mapper for the audience you set.

A hub assertion is `typ` `fb-assert+jwt`, EdDSA, `iss` `fireball-hub`,
`aud` the configured audience (the Hub module sends `hotloop`), unexpired, signed
by a key in the Hub's JWKS. There is no `jti` replay cache: one tool call is
several HTTP requests (initialize, then the call) carrying the same assertion,
which lives 60 s. When the Hub says the call acts for someone else
(`acting_as`), the actor reads `mcp:<email> for <acting_as email>`.

Writes still need `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES`, the master switch; a
token never widens it. `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_WRITE_ROLE` narrows them per caller:
`hotloop:hotloop.write` means the Vord client role `hotloop.write` on client
`hotloop` (`resource_access.hotloop.roles`), a bare name means a realm role, and
a Hub assertion must carry the role's name in `abilities`. A caller without it
can read but `write_tag`, `call_service`, `run_script`, `apply_recipe`,
`trigger_automation` and every tool that changes configuration refuse. The static token is not limited by it.

### Over stdio

The same binary serves MCP on stdin and stdout with `--mcp-stdio`, for a client
that spawns it directly. Everything else starts too, so the agent sees a live
plant rather than a hollow server.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hotloop": {
      "command": "/usr/local/bin/hotloop",
      "args": ["--mcp-stdio"],
      "env": {
        "HOTLOOP_DB_HOST": "timescale.plant.local",
        "HOTLOOP_DB_PASSWORD": "…"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

In stdio mode all logging goes to stderr. Anything written to stdout would
corrupt the protocol stream.

## Tools

One hundred and seventy-one of them: twenty-seven that read the plant and command it, sixty-nine that change its configuration ([below](#changing-configuration)), thirty-three reads and dry runs that go with them ([below](#reads-and-dry-runs)) and forty-two for administration ([below](#administration)).

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `get_plant_status` | devices online, alarms outstanding, whether writes are enabled |
| `list_devices` | every device with protocol, address, state, tag count |
| `describe_device` | one device in detail, with its tags and poll statistics |
| `list_tags` | search the catalog by device, name or description |
| `read_tag` | current values, with quality |
| `query_history` | historical readings, raw or bucketed |
| `write_tag` | **command a tag** |
| `list_alarms` | alarms and their ISA-18.2 states |
| `ack_alarm` | acknowledge on an operator's behalf |
| `list_automations` | rules, run counts, last outcome |
| `trigger_automation` | run a rule now |
| `describe_protocol` | what this build actually speaks |
| `recent_events` | the system log, to work out what happened in what order |
| `list_entities` | find entities by domain, equipment node or label, with the services each takes |
| `get_states` | current state of one or more entities, with quality and attributes |
| `call_service` | **command an entity**: `switch.turn_on`, `number.set_value` |
| `get_logbook` | one timeline of state changes, writes, alarms, runs and config changes, by entity, equipment node, actor or kind |
| `list_scripts` | the plant's scripts, the fields each takes, whether it is running, its last run |
| `run_script` | **run a script**, or ask with `dryRun` what it would do right now |
| `list_recipes` | the plant's recipes: targets in order, parameters, precondition, version, last application |
| `validate_recipe` | would a recipe apply right now? every reason it would be refused; nothing written |
| `apply_recipe` | **apply a recipe**: checked whole, written in order, read back |
| `list_blueprints` | the blueprints people fill in to make rules, their inputs and versions |
| `preview_blueprint` | the rule a blueprint would make with given inputs, and what it would do now; makes nothing |
| `find_network_client` | where a device is on the plant network: its switch port, whether the port has a link, when the UniFi console last saw it |
| `get_network_topology` | the plant network as the UniFi console draws it: what is plugged into what, each device's state, and the HotLoop devices that lose their network if it goes down |
| `get_network_events` | the newest events a UniFi console has reported, and whether its events websocket is live |

### Entities

An entity is what people call a thing on the plant, `sensor.zone_1_temperature`
or `switch.conveyor_run`, wrapping one or more tags. See
[Entities](/iot/entities/). For an agent they are usually the better handle:
the name means something, and the entity knows what you can do to it.

`list_entities` filters by `domain`, by `equipment` (a node of the equipment
tree by id, name or path of names like `Plant A/Packing`, matching everything
at or under it, an entity's own place winning over its device's), by `label`
(label_id or name; an entity matches if it carries the label or its device
does) and by `query`, a substring of the entity_id or name. Each result carries
its current state and quality and the services it takes, as `domain.service`.
An entity with no services is read-only. The services come from the entity
layer, so a domain that gains one there shows up here with no change.

`get_states` takes `entity_ids` and answers each with its state, quality,
attributes and `last_changed`. It holds the same line `read_tag` does: an
`unknown` or `unavailable` state is answered with a note saying it is not a
value, a disabled entity says it is disabled rather than missing, and bad
quality is spelled out.

`call_service` takes `domain`, `service`, `entity_id`, `data` and a **required**
`reason`:

```
> call_service domain=number service=set_value entity_id=number.press_01_sp
    data={"value": 212.5} reason="operator asked for 212.5 on zone 1"
Called number.set_value on number.press_01_sp (was 210). Writes: 212.5 to press-01/Setpoint: written
```

It goes through `entity.Services`, the same runner `POST /api/services/...`
uses, which turns the call into writes through the write gate. See
[Writing](#writing).

### The network

`find_network_client` answers the first question about a PLC that went
quiet: is it the PLC, or its switch port? Give it `deviceId` and it follows
that device's confirmed link to its UniFi client; give it `query` (a MAC, an
IP or part of a name) and it searches every console HotLoop reads. It reads
the UniFi driver's last read, never the console, so an agent asking in a loop
costs the console nothing. That also means an `--mcp-stdio` helper answers
that no console is read in its process: it never logs in to one, because the
Gateway beside it already holds the session. Ask the Gateway's endpoint. See
[UniFi Network](/iot/unifi/).

`get_network_topology` is the map: each switch, access point and gateway under
the one it is plugged into, with the port on both ends, the link, how many
clients are on it, and the HotLoop devices linked to a client below it. That
last part is the blast radius: it names the PLCs that lose their network if
that switch goes. A switch the console lists as plugged into nothing says so
and is not hung off the gateway. `get_network_events` is the console's newest
events, newest first, with its own sentence, a warning flag where the console
calls it negative, and whether the events websocket is live. Both take the
console's `deviceId`, which can be left out when HotLoop reads only one, and
both read the driver's last read like `find_network_client`, so they cost the
console nothing and say the same thing in an `--mcp-stdio` helper: no console
is read in that process. Older events are in `get_logbook`, filed under the
switch or access point they were about.

### The logbook

`get_logbook` is the timeline `GET /api/logbook` serves (see
[The logbook](/iot/logbook/)): state changes, writes, alarm transitions,
automation runs and configuration changes, newest first. It narrows by
`entity`, by `equipment` (id, name or path, and everything under it; a name
that matches two nodes is an error listing both), by `actor` (part of it:
`mcp:` finds everything any agent did), by `kinds`, and by `minutes` back
(default a day). A page with more after it ends by saying what to pass as
`before` for the next. For "what happened before this went wrong" it is the
better `recent_events`: the equipment's own state changes are in it, and the
write gate's lines are not in it twice.

### Scripts

A script is a named sequence of steps somebody wrote once, the CIP cycle or
the line purge, so an agent runs the plant's own procedure instead of making
one up. See [Scripts](/iot/scripts/). `list_scripts` says what each takes.
`run_script` takes `scriptId`, `fields`, a **required** `reason`, and two
switches:

- `dryRun: true` walks the script against the plant as it is and says, step
  by step, what would be written and the first thing the gate would refuse,
  in the gate's words. Nothing is written or audited. Ask this first.
- `wait: true` answers once the run has ended, with its outcome and trace.
  Without it the answer is the run id, and `list_scripts` or `get_logbook`
  with `kinds: ["script"]` says how it ended.

The run is the script's, as `script:<id>`, with the source `mcp`, so every
write it makes meets the gate exactly like `write_tag`. With writes switched
off (`HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES`), `run_script` refuses before anything runs, the way
`trigger_automation` does; a dry run is still answered, and says the switch is
why.

### Recipes

A recipe is a set of setpoints the plant applies together, a product grade or
a changeover, so an agent loads the plant's own numbers instead of writing
them one at a time. See [Recipes](/iot/recipes/). `list_recipes` shows each
one's targets in order and the parameters it takes. `validate_recipe` asks
whether one would apply right now and gives every reason it would not,
writing nothing. `apply_recipe` takes `recipeId`, `params`, an optional
`version` and a **required** `reason`.

It is checked whole first and refused whole, with nothing written, if any
value would be refused; values out of range are refused, never adjusted. Then
the targets go out in order under one call id, the first that fails stops the
rest, and nothing is undone. The answer says, target by target, what went out
and whether the device read the value back. The writes are the agent's, with
the source `mcp`, so the gate applies to each; with writes switched off
(`HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES`), `apply_recipe` refuses before anything is checked. A recipe that names its own apply permission is for the people
granted it, and an agent is not one of them.

### Blueprints

A blueprint is a rule written once with typed blanks in it: which motor, how
long, what limit. See [Blueprints](/iot/blueprints/). `list_blueprints` says
what each one takes. `preview_blueprint` takes `blueprintId`, `automationId`
and `inputs`, and answers the rule it would make and what that rule would do
if it fired right now, every write put to the gate's checks. The inputs are
checked exactly as the screen checks them: out of range is refused, not
adjusted.

`instantiate_blueprint` makes the rule, through the route the Blueprints screen
uses: the same checks, and the rule lands in the logbook with the agent as who
made it. A rule is a standing order to command equipment every time its trigger
fires, so an agent looks first: `preview_blueprint` stores nothing and writes
nothing, and is answered whether or not writes are on. Every write the made rule
goes on to make meets the write gate, as for a rule a person made. See
[Changing configuration](#changing-configuration).

## Changing configuration

Everything an agent can read, it can change. The tools above that read the plant
have counterparts that change it, sixty-nine of them, and none of them is a
second implementation: each is one route of the REST API, and a call is run
through that route's own handler. The validation, the permission check, the
runtime reload and the audit line are the route's, with the agent as the actor
(`mcp:<client>`, or `mcp:<email>` with a Vord login), so a device with no driver,
a rule that does not compile, a blueprint input out of range or a tag the
discovered device has not been accepted for are refused in the words the screen
shows, and nothing was changed.

Each takes the route's path values by name (`id`, `device`, `name`...), `body`,
the same JSON the API takes ([The HTTP API](/iot/api/) has every body), and a **required**
`reason`. The reason is recorded as a `config` line in the system log next to the
route's own, against the thing changed.

```
> save_tag reason="the setpoint, writable between 0 and 100" body={"deviceId":"press-01",
    "name":"Setpoint","address":"holding:5:uint16","dataType":"int16","enabled":true,
    "writable":true,"hasRange":true,"minValue":0,"maxValue":100}
save_tag done.
{ ...the tag as stored... }
```

What stands in front of them is what stands in front of `write_tag`, less the
master switch, because the screens do not need it to change configuration either:

1. `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_MCP_WRITES`, on by default, must be on.
2. A caller with `HOTLOOP_MCP_OIDC_WRITE_ROLE` set must hold it.
3. The call carries one permission, the one its route asks for (the third column
   below), and nothing else. A route answers an agent as it answers a person
   without that permission, and a test holds every row of the table to a real
   route and the permission that route asks for.
4. A reason.

Commanding equipment is still `write_tag`, `call_service`, `run_script`,
`apply_recipe` and `trigger_automation` with `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES` on and the
tag's writable mark and range to meet. Making a tag writable, a rule, a script or
a recipe is configuration: it commands nothing until it is used, and what it
commands then goes through the gate.

The administrator's own functions are tools too, under [Administration](#administration)
below. Accepting a discovered device is here, as it is on the screen; the points
on it still have to be armed for writing one at a time.

The tools exist in `--mcp-stdio` as well: the process builds the same API server,
and never opens its port.

`import_codesys_alarms` takes the file the CODESYS IDE's Export Alarms wrote, as
`contentBase64` (the bytes as they are on disk, which the IDE writes as UTF-16) or
as `content` (the text, if you have it as text), with the `deviceId` the alarms belong to and, if you
want them, `application` and `defaultPriority`. Left alone it only previews: it
says which alarms would come across and which would not, saves nothing, and needs
no reason. With `apply` true it saves them as alarm definitions, and then it needs
a reason and the MCP write switch like every tool that changes configuration.

`screen_export` answers a dashboard as a HotLoop screen file ([Screen files](/iot/screen-file/)),
and `screen_import` takes one in, on this install or another. It asks first:
`dryRun` is true unless you say false, and a dry run saves nothing and answers the
report with every problem listed and the references to `remap`. A real import
needs `dryRun` false, a reason and the MCP write switch, and an id that exists is
refused unless `replace` is true. The screen is the customer's data, so the file
is the way it moves between installs, never code.

### Reads and dry runs

An agent that can change a dashboard, a broker or a node of the equipment tree
has to be able to read what is there first, so each object a tool above changes
has a read here, and the editors' dry runs are tools too. Each is one route run
through its own handler with the read permission that route asks for. A read
answers without a reason and without the write switch, and a caller the write role
leaves out can still make them, because they carry a read permission and nothing
more. The three dry runs (`validate_automation`, `validate_script` and
`browse_device`) change nothing; the two that check a body carry the write
permission their route asks for, so they stay behind the write role.

| Tool | Route | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| `list_alarm_definitions` | `GET /api/alarms` | `alarms.read` |
| `list_composite_entities` | `GET /api/entities/composites` | `entities.read` |
| `list_energy_meters` | `GET /api/energy/meters` | `energy.read` |
| `get_energy_meter` | `GET /api/energy/meters/{id}` | `energy.read` |
| `get_energy_summary` | `GET /api/energy/summary/{period}` | `energy.read` |
| `get_energy_series` | `GET /api/energy/series/{meter}/{period}/{step}` | `energy.read` |
| `list_alarm_events` | `GET /api/alarms/events` | `alarms.read` |

### Administration

User accounts, settings, backups, the escalation policy, the historian targets,
the broker logins, the fleet of edge relays and scheduled reports are the
administrator's, and they are tools as well: forty-two of them, the same
pattern as the rest. Each is one route run through its own handler with the
permission that route asks for (`users.manage`, `settings.write`, `backup.run`,
`fleet.restart`...), a reason for every change and the agent in the audit line.
A route that refuses refuses an agent in the same words. The reads (the `list_`
and `get_` tools) need no reason and no write switch, and still need the
caller's write role when one is set, because the permission they carry is an
administrator's. The fleet and report tools exist only in a product that has the
feature.

Two things are the routes' own and worth knowing before relying on a tool:

- **The write switches have no route.** `safety.allowWrites` and
  `safety.allowMcpWrites` are the deployment's (`HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES`,
  `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_MCP_WRITES`), and `PUT /api/settings` refuses them as set by the
  deployment. So `save_settings` changes what the Settings screen can change and
  answers that refusal for the switches, in those words. An agent cannot turn on
  the switch its own writes wait on.
- **A user's password goes through the call.** `create_user`, `reset_user_password`
  and the PIN tools take a secret in their arguments, as the API does. The audit
  line names the change and the reason and never the secret.

## Resources

| URI | Contents |
|---|---|
| `iiot://devices` | the device tree with tags, as JSON |
| `iiot://tags` | the tag catalog with current values |
| `iiot://alarms` | alarm definitions, live state, and a state reference |
| `iiot://protocols` | supported protocols, from the compiled-in drivers |

Resources exist so a client can pull the whole namespace in one read rather than
discovering it a tool call at a time.

## What the tools will not do

The tools are written so that a model cannot round off uncertainty by accident.

**A tag with no reading is not a tag reading zero.** `read_tag` says
`no reading has been taken for this tag yet`, or `this tag is not configured` if
it does not exist. Neither returns a value.

**Bad quality is stated, not implied.** Readings come back as
`[quality: bad (the value is NOT known; do not treat it as a measurement)]`. The
server instructions repeat it. Do not average across bad readings and do not
report one as a measurement.

**`describe_protocol` cannot lie.** Availability comes from the drivers compiled
into the binary, so the tool cannot claim a protocol the gateway does not have.

**A refusal is an answer, not a transport failure.** A refused write comes back
as a tool result with `isError`, meaning the call was well-formed and
deliberately declined. It is not a protocol error to be retried.

## Writing

MCP reads and writes: it commands equipment, and it changes configuration
([above](#changing-configuration)). `write_tag` moves real equipment, so the same things stand
between a tool call and a machine that stand between an operator's click and one:

1. `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES`, the master switch for the whole deployment, must be
   on. With it off nothing writes: not the UI, not the API, not an agent.
2. The tag must be marked writable. Tags are read-only until somebody says
   otherwise, one at a time.
3. The value must be within the tag's configured range. It is **rejected, not
   clamped**, sending 400 when someone asked for 500 is quietly doing something
   different from what was asked.

A **reason is required** and is recorded next to the write. An audit row nobody
can interpret six months later is barely better than none.

`call_service` gets exactly the same three, because it is nothing but writes
through the same gate, and then the entity's own checks on top (a number's
step and narrower range, a text's pattern, the entity not being disabled). A
refusal at any of them is audited against the entity as well as the tag:
source `mcp`, the client by name, the entity_id, the service and the call id,
the same row a refused `write_tag` leaves plus the entity. A call without a
reason is refused before anything is attempted, like `write_tag`.

`trigger_automation` is gated identically, because a rule's actions can command
equipment; otherwise it would be a way around the checks `write_tag` meets.

```
> write_tag tag=press-01/Zone1_Temp value=99 reason="testing"
write refused: press-01/Zone1_Temp: this tag is not marked writable
```

When writes are switched off the server instructions say so up front, so an
agent does not waste a turn discovering it.

## Calling out

An automation's `mcp_call` action invokes a tool on another MCP server. Configure
the servers in the chart:

```yaml
mcp:
  outboundServers:
    - name: maintenance
      url: http://maintenance-mcp.default.svc.cluster.local:8080/mcp
      existingSecret: maintenance-mcp-token
      secretKey: token
```

Sessions are pooled and reused; connecting per call would mean a handshake, an
initialize and a tool listing every time a rule fires. A session that has died
is reconnected on the next call rather than on a timer, because the next call is
the first moment anybody cares. A configured server that is down does not stop
the plant being monitored, nothing is dialed until a rule needs it.

The MCP screen shows each configured server, whether it is connected, and the
tools it advertises.

## Federating sites

One gateway per plant is how this is meant to run. Each site keeps its own
database, its own board and its own name, and none of them depend on a link to
anywhere else staying up, a plant does not stop being monitored because the WAN
dropped.

Seeing all of them at once uses the protocol the sites already speak. Configure
a gateway at the cloud with the sites as outbound MCP servers, exactly as for the
`mcp_call` action:

```
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_1_NAME=akron
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_1_URL=https://akron.example/mcp
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_1_TOKEN=…
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_2_NAME=ashtabula
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_2_URL=https://ashtabula.example/mcp
HOTLOOP_MCP_SERVER_2_TOKEN=…
```

The Sites screen then calls `get_plant_status` on each of them in parallel and
rolls the answers up. There is nothing to deploy at a site to make it appear, no
site has to know it is federated, and nothing connects inward to a plant network.

Two behaviors are deliberate and worth relying on:

- A site that does not answer is shown as **unreachable, with the reason**, and
  is left out of the roll-up. Counting a plant you cannot reach as zero alarms is
  the worst thing a screen like this could do.
- The numbers a site last reported are never shown. They look current and are not.

Each site gets its own short deadline, so one plant on a dead link cannot hold up
the ones that are up.

## Worth telling an agent

The server's own instructions cover this, but for anyone writing a prompt around
it:

- Alarm states follow ISA-18.2. `rtn-unack` means an alarm cleared on its own
  before anybody saw it, it is still worth reporting, and it is the state that
  proves acknowledgement and return-to-normal are independent.
- `query_history` with buckets, not raw, for anything longer than a few minutes.
  A day of one-second data is 86,400 points per tag. Buckets follow
  the quality rule: bad and uncertain readings
  are counted in `badReadings`, never averaged in, and a bucket with nothing
  good has a null average.
- `recent_events` is the way to reconstruct an incident: device connections,
  writes, alarm transitions, automation runs and configuration changes, in order,
  each with the actor that caused it.
